subject: english-language
title: Commas, Colons, Semicolons
welcome_lead: Mid-sentence marks shape meaning and pace.
meta_desc: KS3 English Language adventure on commas, colons and semicolons.
final_note: You can now use commas, colons and semicolons correctly.

concepts.def: Pair of commas around extra info.

walkthroughs.body_html: Use listing commas: 'apples, pears, plums'. Use bracketing commas around extra info: 'My uncle, the doctor, agreed.'
A colon introduces ('You need: bread, jam, butter.'). A semicolon joins two related sentences ('I was tired; I went home.').
Apostrophes show missing letters ('don't') or possession ('Tom's bag'). Don't use them for normal plurals.

mcqs.q: Which mark joins two related sentences?
What is the difference between inflectional and derivational morphology?
options: Inflectional morphology applies only to verbs and derivational only to nouns.
Inflection and derivation are two words for the same process.
Because English speakers have always wanted to make things complicated.

Inflectional morphemes mark grammatical features without changing word class (cat/cats, walk/walked); derivational morphemes create new words, often changing word class (happy → happiness, teach → teacher).

mcqs.q: What is the difference between voiced and voiceless sounds?
options: Inflectional morphology applies only to verbs and derivational only to nouns.
Voiced sounds are loud and voiceless sounds are whispered.
Voiced sounds are produced with vocal-fold vibration (/b/, /d/, /g/, /z/); voiceless sounds without it (/p/, /t/, /k/, /s/). You can feel the difference by putting a hand on your throat.
Voiced sounds use the lips; voiceless sounds use the tongue.

mcqs.q: Why does English vocabulary have so many synonyms?
options: Layered historical contact — Old English, Old Norse, Norman French and Latin — left English with multiple words from different sources for similar concepts (e.g. ask/question/interrogate).
Voiced sounds use the lips; voiceless sounds use the tongue.
Because English speakers have always wanted to make things complicated.
English has many synonyms because Shakespeare invented lots of words.
